teaser: 28 supply-chain attacks read as reach beyond mandate: what a hardened registry stops, what only a written mandate can, and why agents change it.
core_idea: Every incident in a public ledger of 28 supply-chain attacks is a credential, tag or build step that could do more than it was meant to, so consumer-side controls a registry sells would likely have held in 26 and publisher-side mandates in 16; as agents become the maintainers that hold tokens and add dependencies, the pipeline needs three records, trusted inputs, a written mandate and provable outputs with memory, and small open source projects need a path onto the trusted list.

figures.caption: The ledger. Chainguard's 28 public supply-chain incidents, May 2024 to October 2026, each dot one incident, coloured by its first vector; 23 of them are from 2026. Below, every vector counted, by our reading: an install-time hook ran the payload in 17, a maintainer account or token was taken over in 16.

For each of the 28 incidents, the control that would most likely have stopped it, by our reading: on the consumer's side, what you let in; on the publisher's side, what a credential was for. A consumer-side control appears in 26, a publisher-side mandate in 16, both in 14. And one case where the consumer was a model.
One pipeline, three records: what an agent consumes, what it was allowed to do, and what it produced and remembers. The first has products; the second and third are what RiskMandate and sgit work on.
